 On the campaign trail
 • 3 days to go : President Donald Trump won’t hold in-person campaign events today, instead planning telerallies to try to reach more voters. While he reinstated events in Iowa and Kansas on Sunday, he complained yesterday that his voice was wearing down and he wasn’t sure more rallies would help.
 • Michigan divisions : Democratic Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed’s campaign has asked primary rival Haley Stevens to stay away from his remaining events, a source tells CNN. That calls into question a previously expected joint appearance Sunday in Detroit.
 • What happens in Alaska: Ranked-choice voting and mail-in balloting across the state means a critical Senate race could take weeks to resolve . Now, ramped-up federal and state investigations into Democrat Mary Peltola’s campaign could create new complications.

 Judge imposes emergency order halting DOJ pressure campaign on election officials
 By Tierney Sneed 
 A federal judge imposed a sweeping emergency order halting various aggressive tactics employed by the Trump administration in recent days to pressure election officials across the country.
 “Although Defendants claim that their actions are designed to halt unlawful voting by noncitizens, their actions are likely to have the effect of interfering with election administration and disenfranchising lawful voters,” US District Judge Trina Thompson said in her opinion granting a temporary restraining order Friday evening.
 She said, while her order is in place, the Justice Department and the Department of Homeland Security cannot demand that election officials in any state segregate ballots, purge voters from voter rolls, or halt ballot processing.
 Thompson, who was appointed by President Joe Biden, is also blocking threats of criminal prosecutions against election officials from those agencies and said that the administration cannot take other actions that “threaten, intimidate or coerce” election officials to demand changes in ballot processing procedures on claims the voters are ineligible.
 Thompson’s opinion rebuked claims the administration has made for months that it can and will prosecute election officials for not doing enough to prevent illegal voting.

 Stevens was asked to stay away from El-Sayed's events, source says
 By Eric Bradner 
 Michigan Democratic Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed’s campaign has asked his former primary opponent, Rep. Haley Stevens, to skip all campaign events in the race’s closing days, a person familiar with the matter said.
 That means a planned Sunday show of unity — with the two appearing at a Detroit church with South Carolina Rep. Jim Clyburn — is now likely to exclude Stevens. It would have been her first time appearing alongside El-Sayed since their heated August primary.

 Mike Nellis: 'I think it's sour grapes from Haley Stevens... this is absolutely ridiculous' 
 2:22
 Politico first reported that the El-Sayed campaign had asked the congresswoman to stay away from events. Stevens did not immediately respond to a request for comment about her plans.
 Some context: The news comes after the two traded barbs Friday . Stevens called on El-Sayed to denounce an outside group’s controversial advertisement that blames US foreign aid for Israel for Americans’ struggles with high costs. El-Sayed responded that Stevens “seems intent on relitigating a primary that ended three months ago.” El-Sayed is a vocal critic of Israel’s actions in Gaza and of the United States’ financial backing of Israel’s military.
 Criticism: State Sen. Mallory McMorrow, who also ran in the Senate primary but dropped out four weeks before the election, was sharply critical of Stevens , casting her actions as disruptive to Democrats’ chances of defeating Republican former Rep. Mike Rogers and retaining a Senate seat that is crucial to the battle for majority control of the chamber next Tuesday.
 “I have no idea what the hell Haley Stevens is doing. This is a moment where we have to recognize the stakes,” McMorrow said.
 GOP rival tries to court Democrats: Meanwhile, Rogers on Friday accused El-Sayed of “vile racism and antisemitism” and said Democrats who backed Stevens have “a home with us.”

 Trump says Attorney General to "make his own decision" on potential actions in Alaska voting controversy 
 1:13
 President Donald Trump rallied supporters in Daytona Beach, Florida yesterday evening, just days before the midterm election. It was his second rally in the state in a week, after appearing in Fort Myers last Friday.
 Florida has trended very Republican in the Trump era. A New York Times/Siena poll released earlier this week showed that the Senate race in the state is not nearly as competitive as in some red states with margin-of-error races.
 Catch up on what he said at the rally:
 ‘Does it matter?’: Further explaining why the rallies in Iowa and Kansas were canceled and then restored to his schedule, Trump said he had questioned whether his presence would even matter. 
 “They called me in Iowa, and they called me in Kansas, and they said, ‘Sir, would it be possible to do a little rally of about 50,000 people each?’ And I said, ‘Does it matter?’ They said, ‘We just want to make sure that we win.’” he said.
 Alaska Senate race: While Trump said Attorney General Todd Blanche would make his own decision about whether Alaska Democrat Mary Peltola should be prosecuted, the president made his own wishes very clear. He was alluding to the criminal probe into whether Alaska Democrats sought to confuse voters by recruiting a candidate intended to siphon votes from Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan.
 “She should be removed from the ballot and prosecuted. But he’s going to make his own decision. I’m not telling you. Todd, please make your own, right,” he said.
 Warning to GOP: Trump urged Florida Republicans to play from behind, warning them not to get too confident ahead of Tuesday.
 “You got to vote. Bad things happen when you get too confident, right? So let’s pretend they’re one point down,” he told the rally crowd.
 CNN’s Julia Benbrook, Kit Maher and Aleena Fayaz contributed reporting.

 Trump's rallies this weekend are back on — after an abrupt about-face
 By Molly English 
 President Donald Trump takes the stage during a campaign rally at the Ocean Center Arena in Daytona Beach, Florida, on Friday. 
 Andrew Harnik/Getty Images 
 President Donald Trump will hold rallies tomorrow in Kansas and Iowa, he announced Friday, just hours after the White House said he was scrapping the events and opting for a slew of virtual engagements instead.
 Trump has insisted he got calls from people in both Iowa and Kansas urging him to reinstate the in-person rallies.
 “They said, ‘If you could go it would be better than a telerally.’ And I tried to talk them out of that and I said, ‘What about a telerally?’ But they asked me,” Trump told reporters in the Oval Office on Friday, just before departing for a campaign event in Daytona, Florida.
 “So I’m going to do two on Sunday,” he added. “And I was a little bit concerned about Saturday because college football. It’s Iowa, Kansas.”
 How we got here: Trump originally had a rally in Salina, Kansas, planned for Saturday and another in Dubuque, Iowa, on Sunday.
 Those were shifted to telerallies on Thursday, in a confounding last-minute strategy shift that was covered critically in the media, leading to Trump becoming irritated at how the cancellations were being received. The rallies were subsequently revived Friday morning.
 The president insisted Friday that the telerallies are a successful medium for him, saying he’s “unbelievable” and “it only seems to work for me.”
 Trump still plans to stump for several candidates via telerally, and said Friday that he’d call into quite a few of them the day before the election.
